note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Follow a living culm to its full, usually 8–15 cm, loose to moderately open panicle. Long bare proximal portions of fine arching branches lead to groups of spikelets. Existing panels 0–1 illustrate gross architecture; the bare branch section ALSO occurs in purpletop, so it is not decisive alone. Archived CC0 panel 4 now adds a genuine Uvalde County flowering-habitat view; the roots and flowering stems are not traceable as one plant.
tiles.short: Short flexuous panicle; hanging spikelet groups
tiles.status: VISIBLE GROSS STRUCTURE; WHOLE ROOTED PLANT GAP

tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK GROWTH AND COLLAR
tiles.details: Trace flowering stems to a perennial crown; older Texas descriptions give roughly 30–60 cm culms, often bent near base. Open the true inner blade/sheath junction: a very short ligule of hairs, separate from longer throat/collar hairs. Panel 3 is source-labelled as a collar view but has no calibrated ligule measurement; do not infer a precise mm cutoff. Panel 3 is physically archived from Gaiacoyote's source-labelled original; a pale hair fringe is visible but its free margin and length are not calibrated. Panel 4 is habitat, NOT a collar macro.
tiles.short: Perennial tuft; ligule a very short hair ring
tiles.status: REAL ARCHIVED COLLAR-REGION PHOTO; MEASURED LIGULE AND ROOTED CROWN GAPS

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT ONE MATURE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Historical Silveus Texas Grasses treatment gives mature spikelets about 6–11 mm with approximately 6–10 florets. Panel 2 is a source-labelled dissection view, but its scale and floret count are not independently certified here. Keep one entire spikelet attached to a 1-mm ruler before separating bracts. Panel 2 now exists as a physical GitHub JPEG, not merely a remote reference; the glumes and floret count still require calibrated pixel-level verification.
tiles.status: LOCAL SOURCE-LABELLED SPIKELET PHOTO; CALIBRATED MACRO NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES ARE NOT LEMMAS
tiles.details: Historical Silveus treatment: thin 1-veined glumes, lower about 2–3 mm and upper slightly longer; fertile lemma about 4 mm with three veins, hairs below the middle along its nerves, and two tiny apical teeth. Another field account describes glumes approximately lemma-length; this source disagreement prevents a rigid glume:lemma ratio test. The projecting midvein is a minute mucro, not a long awn.

tiles.heading: 05 · COMPARE THE LOCAL TRIDENS
tiles.details: Panels 7–8 are purpletop (T. flavus), which usually has a larger, wider, drooping panicle but can also have empty lower branch segments and pink spikelets. Panels 5–6 are white tridens (T. albescens), generally with narrower crowded appressed heads. Do not confuse these comparison photographs with Texas tridens. Mature glumes and hairy lemma nerves are needed when panicles overlap.
tiles.short: Purpletop overlaps; white tridens is tighter
tiles.status: GROSS LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; MATCHED MACROS MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · PROVE THE ANATOMY BEFORE 100%
tiles.details: To close the card, obtain a voucher-confirmed same-plant series from rooted tuft through flowering head, then one 6–11 mm spikelet and separated glumes/three-veined hairy lemma under 10–40× with millimeter scale. Add arrows only when actual hair lines, glume boundaries and mucro are resolved. Preserve existing photo rights and any Hays nativity holds.
tiles.short: Measure collar, glumes, lemma and tiny mucro

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TEXAS TRIDENS — look for a perennial tuft with a relatively short, loose, FLEXUOUS panicle; slender branches are often bare near their bases and carry hanging groups of multi-flowered spikelets toward their ends. Purpletop can also have bare branch bases and rosy spikelets. Under 10–20× confirm two thin glumes, a three-veined approximately 4-mm lemma hairy along its lower nerves and a tiny midvein mucro, not a long awn. Glume-to-lemma ratios differ among sources; do not identify from a rigid ratio without a measured ripe spikelet.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: See the first SOURCE-LABELLED PHOTO: use gross branches and spikelets as starting clues, not independent expert taxon confirmation.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Trace flowering stems to a perennial crown; older Texas descriptions give roughly 30–60 cm culms, often bent near base. Open the true inner blade/sheath junction: a very short ligule of hairs, separate from longer throat/collar hairs. Panel 3 is source-labelled as a collar view but has no calibrated ligule measurement; do not infer a precise mm cutoff. Panel 3 is physically archived from Gaiacoyote's source-labelled original; a pale hair fringe is visible but its free margin and length are not calibrated. Panel 4 is habitat, NOT a collar macro.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Historical Silveus Texas Grasses treatment gives mature spikelets about 6–11 mm with approximately 6–10 florets. Panel 2 is a source-labelled dissection view, but its scale and floret count are not independently certified here. Keep one entire spikelet attached to a 1-mm ruler before separating bracts. Panel 2 now exists as a physical GitHub JPEG, not merely a remote reference; the glumes and floret count still require calibrated pixel-level verification.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Against T. flavus, both can have open drooping heads and bare proximal branch sections; compare shorter flexuous Texas panicle plus ~1/2-length glumes and lower-half lemma nerve hairs. Against T. albescens, separated drooping branch-end spikelets versus a narrow crowded spike are useful, but mature glume/lemma characters seal the ID. Eragrostis secundiflora can resemble rosy heads; check multi-flowered Tridens spikelet and dorsal three-nerve lemma anatomy.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: ALBESCENS narrow packed; FLAVUS wide drooping; TEXANUS flexuous separated. Confirm at mature GLUMES and 3-NERVED LEMMA.
safety_note: Bare panicle branch bases are not unique to Texas tridens. Source-labelled photos do not establish unreviewed county nativity.
field_rule: Species-level Tridens confidence requires panicle architecture PLUS mature spikelet/glume/lemma anatomy; do not identify from pigmentation alone.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
